idea: Luke Howard's three cloud sketches (cirrus, cumulus, stratus) from his 1803 essay, labelled in his Latin, captioned 'Clouds had no names until a chemist gave them Latin ones. 1802.' For people who look up and want the vocabulary.

One of Wilson Bentley's 1880s-90s snowflake photomicrographs traced to a single-ink plate, captioned 'No two alike. He checked 5,000.' Bentley photographed more than 5,000 flakes; a quiet joke on a famous claim.

The Franklin-Folger Gulf Stream chart (c.1769-70) with the current drawn as a heavy black ribbon, captioned 'A whaler told Franklin. Franklin drew it.' Credit to the Nantucket captain Timothy Folger, for people who like the real origin story.

A crop of Harold Fisk's 1944 Army Corps maps of the lower Mississippi, with the abandoned channels as black ribbons, captioned 'The river was here. And here. And here.' Rivers wander; a pattern pretty enough to wear.

A single drawn meander with a loop being cut off, and Mark Twain's Life on the Mississippi arithmetic: 'The Lower Mississippi has shortened itself 242 miles in 176 years.' True figures, in Twain's own count.

Hiroshige's 'Sudden Shower over Shin-Ohashi Bridge' (1857) rendered as black rain lines on white, captioned 'Chance of rain: 100% since 1857.' The beloved woodblock of people hurrying across a bridge, with a forecaster's deadpan.

A Lichtenberg figure (the branching dust-and-spark pattern first recorded by Georg Lichtenberg in 1777) generated in code, captioned 'Lightning, rivers, lungs, roots. Same tree.' The idea that branching networks keep re-inventing themselves.

The Beaufort scale as a typographic ladder, Force 0 'Calm' to Force 12 'That which no canvas sails could withstand' (Beaufort's own 1805 wording), with a tiny engraved ship shrinking in sail at each rung. For sailors and anyone who likes a good scale.

An old engraved coastline of the British Isles with the shipping-forecast sea areas as its only labels (Viking, Forties, Dogger, Fisher, German Bight, Rockall, Malin, Hebrides), captioned 'Good, occasionally poor.' A bedtime litany for the weather-obsessed.

Admiral Robert FitzRoy's storm-warning cone drawn as a plain engraved plate, captioned 'Admiral FitzRoy coined the word forecast in 1860. People have been annoyed ever since.' Honors the man who gave weather a public voice, and was mocked for it.

Caspar David Friedrich's Wanderer above the Sea of Fog (c.1818) reduced to a black silhouette on a fog of fine stipple, captioned 'Outlook: unclear.' A romantic painting with a weather-forecast punchline.

The Lena River delta traced from public-domain Landsat imagery as one black branching hand, captioned 'Lena River: 4,400 km of thinking, then this.' A river's last sentence, beautiful as a fingerprint.

Punch's 1855 cartoon 'Faraday giving his card to Father Thames' redrawn in line, with its own wording: 'Faraday gives his card to Father Thames.' The Thames was filthy, the scientist was polite, and the Great Stink followed in 1858.

Lewis Fry Richardson's 1922 'forecast factory' drawn in code: a spherical hall of tiny desks and one conductor, captioned '64,000 people to beat the weather.' His imagined human-computer system for numerical forecasting, a century before the supercomputer.

An engraved wind-head cherub from an old map blowing across a list of named winds: 'Mistral. Sirocco. Bora. Tramontane. Levante. Chinook.' With the caption 'Every wind that has a name had somebody to blame.' For people who like weather with a personality.

A drawn wall of stone with a column of tally ticks climbing it, each labelled only with a year, captioned 'The river keeps better records than the council.' Based on the real flood marks cut into old river-town walls.

A Plimsoll line (the circle with the horizontal bar, as marked on ship hulls) drawn clean, captioned 'Don't load past here. Law since 1876.' Samuel Plimsoll's Merchant Shipping Act made the mark compulsory; a gentle shirt about limits.

Leonardo da Vinci's c.1510 drawing of water pouring into a pool and curling into eddies (Royal Collection), with his line 'Observe the motion of the surface of the water, which resembles that of hair.' A 500-year-old note on looking closely, in his own words.

A meandering river drawn in code beside Einstein's 1926 river paper, captioned 'Left alone, a river's length drifts toward π times the straight line.' Einstein linked meanders to tea leaves and Baer's law; a real result, a pleasing number.

An engraved spring welling out of a hillside beside a rain gauge, captioned 'Where do rivers come from? Rain. Pierre Perrault measured it, 1674.' Perrault's Seine measurements showed rainfall could account for river flow, when many still believed in underground seawater.
